title: USMNT erects training ground barriers to guard against World Cup spying
content:
SEATTLE — The U.S. men’s national soccer team positioned barriers on a small hill at its World Cup training facility Saturday in an apparent attempt to ensure that no one could spy on the team’s preparations for a round-of-16 showdown with Belgium.

There is no specific suspicion that Belgium or anyone else was attempting to spy on the team’s training session, a U.S. Soccer spokesman clarified.

But USMNT staff realized that, on elevated ground to the west of Husky Soccer Stadium, where the team is training while in Seattle, there are tall buildings with views of the field.

From McMahon Hall, an undergraduate dormitory on the University of Washington’s campus, for example, if standing on a top-floor balcony or at a window, you can see the entire pitch, according to photos posted on the university’s website.

Those specific balconies are currently closed, and some buildings might be closed for the summer, but there are multiple tall buildings on campus, and perhaps others near it, that potentially offer views of the field.

The barriers set up Wednesday likely would not block all of those views, but they were seemingly stationed strategically to fill gaps in the trees on the west end of the field.

Staffers wheeled the barriers over from the adjacent University of Washington baseball complex. They were screens with netting, the type used for batting practice, with brown tarps tugged over them to make them solid.

Although there is no suspicion of spying in this specific case, there is a long history of espionage in international soccer. Canada’s men’s and women’s national teams infamously used drones to capture footage of opponents training for years until they were caught at the 2024 Olympics.

During the group stage, when the USMNT trained here one day before its match against Australia, head coach Mauricio Pochettino went up to the small hill at Husky Soccer Stadium, pulled out his phone, and appeared to take a 360-degree video.

When asked later that day about the moment, he said: “I wanted to see, because we are in an era of — como se dice, ‘espías?’ — spies.” Then he smiled, and continued: “It was a good opportunity to see. I was doing a video, not a picture, about all around, to share after with (team security officer) Jerry (Rawlins) … to share a little bit to see things. Only I wanted that — to see how the view was from outside.”

A team spokesman later said that Pochettino was joking. But two weeks later, with the team back in Seattle, the screens were set up on the same hill.

The U.S. plays Belgium at Lumen Field on Monday at 5 p.m. local time, 8 p.m. ET (Fox, Telemundo).
